name: Forge
text:
**Decision:** We will build every new package, tab enrichment, or draft element as a single, self-contained "module" that can be dropped into any project without extra setup.

**Why:** This keeps things simple and reusable. A module is easy to test, share, and slot into different tools, which speeds up our work and keeps quality high. It also makes it clear who made it—every module gets stamped "Created by EXCAVA," so credit is automatic.

**Trade-off:** We’re choosing flexibility over speed in some cases. A module might take a little longer to design upfront, but it pays off later when we reuse it or fix issues in one place. The alternative—quick, one-off tweaks—would clutter things and make future work harder.

name: Vet
text: **Pushback:** That’s a tidy idea, but modules can become a dumping ground for half-baked code if we don’t enforce strict boundaries. What if a module grows too big or does too much? Instead, we could split work into *tiny, single-purpose modules* (e.g., one for validation, one for UI) and only combine them when needed. To settle this, we’d need to see a concrete example of how a module would stay lean—and agree on a rule like “no module over 200 lines without a split.”

name: Forge
text:
**Decision:** We will build every new package, tab, or draft element as a single, focused module with a clear, narrow purpose—like a "validation helper" or a "UI button"—and keep them small enough to fit in one file.

**Why:** Tiny modules are easier to test, reuse, and swap out if they break or become outdated. They force us to think clearly about what each piece *actually* does, which prevents bloated, hard-to-maintain code. This also makes it simpler for others to grab just what they need without dragging in extra baggage.

**Trade-off:** We accept that some projects will need many small modules instead of a few big ones, which could mean more files to manage. But the clarity and flexibility are worth it—we’d rather fix a dozen tiny modules than untangle one giant one later.

name: Vet
text: **Pushback:** Tiny modules sound neat, but they risk turning every project into a sprawling maze of micro-files where nothing works together unless you wire up a dozen imports. Instead, we could set a *size cap*—say, 200 lines per module—and enforce it with a simple rule: if a module grows past that, we split it *only* when two clear, independent behaviors emerge. That keeps things lean without drowning us in fragments. What would settle this? A quick test: take the smallest module we’ve built so far and see if splitting it further actually makes maintenance easier—or just adds noise.

name: Nova
text:
DECISION: We will build every new package, tab, or draft element as a single, focused module with a clear purpose, but capped at 200 lines—if it grows past that, we split it into smaller, single-purpose modules.

The result must deliver: reusable, testable, and maintainable modules that fit neatly into any project without overwhelming it. Vet owns the enforcement of the size cap and the final call on splits.
